title: Events and Streams
summary: React to events with EventEmitter, then process data of any size piece by piece with readable, writable and transform streams, readline and pipeline.
introduction: Two ideas run through all of Node's core modules. The first is the event: an object announces that something happened (`'data'`, `'close'`, `'error'`) and any number of listeners react. The second is the stream: data arrives in chunks over time instead of all at once, so a 10 GB log file or a slow network upload can be processed with a few kilobytes of memory. HTTP requests, file handles, sockets and compression all use both. This lesson builds the mental model with small, complete examples.
learningObjectives: Emit and listen for events with EventEmitter, including once and error
Read a large file line by line without loading it into memory
Connect readable, transform and writable streams safely with pipeline

blocks.text: `EventEmitter` from `node:events` is the base class behind servers, sockets and streams. `on(name, listener)` registers a function, `emit(name, ...args)` calls every listener for that name in registration order, and `once` registers a listener that removes itself after its first call:

blocks.title: orders.js
node orders.js
blocks.content:
Kitchen: prepare 2 x coffee
Marketing: first order of the day!
Kitchen: prepare 1 x tea
Listeners left: 1

blocks.text: Listeners run **synchronously** inside `emit`: by the time `emit` returns, every listener has finished. Emitters are how you decouple code. The checkout module does not need to know that marketing, the kitchen and an analytics logger all care about orders; it just emits. Your own classes can `extends EventEmitter` to get the same API, and `off(name, listener)` removes a listener you no longer need.

blocks.title: An unhandled error event crashes the process
blocks.text: `'error'` is special: if an emitter emits it and nobody is listening, Node throws the error and the program exits with `Unhandled 'error' event`. Streams, servers and sockets all emit `'error'`, so every one you create needs an error listener (or must be wrapped in `pipeline`, which adds one for you).

`readFile` from the previous lesson waits until the whole file is in memory. That is fine for a config file and disastrous for a multi-gigabyte export: the process either runs out of memory or sits idle for seconds before it can start working. A **stream** delivers the data in chunks (64 KiB by default for files) as soon as each chunk is available, so memory stays flat and work starts immediately. Node has four kinds: **Readable** (a file being read, an incoming request), **Writable** (a file being written, an outgoing response), **Duplex** (both, such as a socket) and **Transform** (a Duplex that changes data on the way through, such as gzip).
Reading a file line by line

Readable streams are async iterables, so `for await` consumes them chunk by chunk. Chunks do not respect line boundaries, though, and the `node:readline` module fixes that by turning any readable stream into an iterable of lines. Save the five-line log below as `access.log`:

blocks.title: count-errors.js

blocks.text: The same program handles a file with fifty million lines; only one line is in memory at a time. `crlfDelay: Infinity` makes Windows line endings (`\r\n`) count as a single line break.

Most stream programs are a chain: read from somewhere, transform, write somewhere else. `pipeline` from `node:stream/promises` connects the pieces, forwards errors from any stage, closes everything properly and returns a promise. It also handles **backpressure**: if the writer is slower than the reader (a slow disk, a slow client), the reader is paused until the writer catches up, so memory never balloons. blocks.text: You will also see `source.pipe(destination)` in older code. It works, but it does not forward errors or clean up when one stage fails, which is why `pipeline` is the recommended form today.

A `Transform` receives each chunk, does something with it and pushes the result on. The `transform(chunk, encoding, callback)` method calls `callback(null, output)` when it is done (or `callback(error)` to fail). `process.stdin` and `process.stdout` are streams too, so a transform can become a classic command-line filter:

blocks.title: HTTP is streams all the way down
blocks.text: In the next lesson the incoming request is a Readable stream (that is why a request body is read with `for await`) and the response is a Writable stream, which is why `res.end()` is needed to finish it. Everything you learned here applies directly.

questions.question: What does this program print?
questions.explanation: Listeners run in registration order on every emit; the once listener runs on the first emit only and is then removed, so the second emit reaches only the on listener.

questions.question: Why is `pipeline` preferred over chaining `.pipe()` calls?
questions.explanation: pipeline forwards an error from any stage, destroys every stream in the chain on failure and returns a promise; plain pipe leaves streams open and errors unhandled when a stage fails.
